title: try , try? , and try!
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of try , try? , and try! in a Swift program or workflow.
Apply using try in a small, inspectable example.
Check the expected result and identify one boundary case or platform constraint.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on try , try? , and try! and the practical choices around it. Start with the smallest example, connect it to “Using try”, and verify the result before adding complexity.
content.why_it_matters: Reusable functions and precise data models reduce duplication. Handling missing data and failures explicitly makes later application code safer to change.

content_blocks.title: Module 7: Optionals and Error Handling
content_blocks.alt_text: Module 7: Optionals and Error Handling. Lessons in order: Introduction to Optionals; Unwrapping Optionals; Optional Binding with guard let; Optional Chaining; Nil-Coalescing and Optional Transformation; Implicitly Unwrapped Optionals; Introduction to Error Handling; Handling Errors with do-catch; try , try? , and try!; Error Handling Design.
content_blocks.caption: Numbered overview of the Optionals and Error Handling learning sequence.

content_blocks.text: **Start with the rule.** For using try, identify the contract, the valid inputs, and the failure or boundary case. Write the smallest reusable Swift example that makes those decisions visible.

**Work through the lesson.** Represent absence with optionals and operation failures with errors; choose the right recovery path. The detailed subtopic list in this lesson preserves the curriculum coverage; treat each item as a cue for a small example or a focused question rather than trying to memorize syntax.

items.title: Using try
items.text: For using try, identify the contract, the valid inputs, and the failure or boundary case. Write the smallest reusable Swift example that makes those decisions visible.

items.title: Converting errors into optionals with try?
items.text: An optional explicitly represents a value that may be absent. Check and bind it before using the wrapped value; avoid forced unwraps unless an invariant is proven.

items.title: Forced error handling with try!
items.text: Use typed errors for operations that can fail and handle them at a boundary that can recover or explain the failure. Do not silently discard meaningful errors.

items.title: Choosing the correct error-handling strategy

content_blocks.title: Keep in mind
content_blocks.text: Use the compiler and versioned documentation as evidence. Do not treat a source-string check or an illustrative output as proof that a complete Swift program compiles on every platform.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming every Swift snippet can run in a browser or on every operating system.
common_mistakes.why: CodeLeaf’s current preview is not a Swift compiler, and Apple frameworks require appropriate target support.
common_mistakes.fix: Run command-line examples locally; use Xcode or a compatible package/target for framework-specific material.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating an illustrative output as compiler verification.
common_mistakes.why: A reference result helps reason about behavior but cannot replace compiling and testing the exact code.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the example with the stated toolchain and test one realistic edge case.

common_mistakes.why: Swift concurrency checks and newer APIs can vary by language mode and toolchain.
common_mistakes.fix: Read the exact diagnostic and confirm the supported version before changing safety checks.
